title: The Stories We Tell Ourselves About Problems
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article explores an often-invisible influence on problem-solving: the private narrative a leader tells themselves about a problem before they even begin devising a strategy. It argues that this internal story — 'I've seen this before,' 'this problem is beyond our capabilities,' 'this can only be managed, not resolved' — quietly shapes the eventual approach, often without the leader consciously noticing. The piece lists several common problem-narratives leaders default to and explains how each one narrows or expands the range of strategies considered. It concludes that the best problem-solvers make this hidden story explicit, interrogate it, and are willing to suspend it in favor of one that opens up better options.
points: Before a strategy forms, leaders unconsciously tell themselves a private story about the nature of the problem.
This story shapes the eventual approach even though it's rarely made explicit or examined.
Common defaulted stories include 'this problem can only be managed, not resolved' or 'this is beyond our capabilities.'
The best problem-solvers make their story explicit and interrogate whether it's helping or limiting them.
Suspending a limiting story can allow a more productive one, and a better strategy, to emerge.
quotes: How leaders approach a problem unquestionably impacts the potential outcome.
The first influence on any problem is the story leaders tell themselves about the problem itself.
A story of experience with a problem typically produces confidence and a readiness for action that can serve a leader well or poorly.
As they repeat this story in their head, they further narrow the strategy or approach they might take to address the problem.
The best problem-solvers understand this and make this step explicit.
Knowing that stories about the problem exert a tremendous influence on any strategy suggests leaders must think deeply about their thinking.
